item.title: See the Menu for the State Dinner Honoring Xi Jinping
item.description:
President Trump and the first lady, Melania Trump, are preparing to host President Xi Jinping of China for a state dinner in the East Room of the White House on Thursday evening.

According to the three-course menu released by the White House, the dishes were chosen to emphasize American ingredients with a “subtle Chinese influence.”

Chefs will serve Mr. Trump, Mr. Xi and other guests a main course of sesame-crusted sea bass and crisp baby bok choy. The yellow squash appetizer will be drizzled with scallion oil. According to the White House, the dishes bring “the culinary traditions of both nations together.”

The East Room tables will be laid with red linens and its urns filled with red blossoms, which the administration said was a reference to the color’s significance in China. “The décor for the evening is an expression of warmth and celebration,” it said.

Diners will begin their meal by toasting with a glass of Schramsberg. That is the California sparkling wine that President Richard M. Nixon drank in 1972 during his visit to Beijing, which heralded a historic thaw in U.S.-Chinese relations.

Yellow squash velouté

Wild mushroom fricassee

Crispy pancetta

Scallion oil

Sesame-crusted sea bass

Braised baby bok choy

Roasted garden eggplant

Sauce verte

Vanilla crémeux and White House honey ice cream

Walnut frangipane

Sour cherry confit

The opera singer Christopher Macchio, who performed this month at the Republican’s midterm convention in Dallas, will headline the evening’s musical lineup.

Military musicians from the U.S. Army and Marine Corps will also perform.

item.title: In Alaska, Rowdy Members of Congress Are a Tradition
item.description:
One threatened a fellow congressman at knife point in a dispute over pet spending projects.

Another routinely wore an Incredible Hulk tie to the Capitol in a proud acknowledgment of his foul temper when he wasn’t getting his way.

Revelations about the conduct of former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat, toward her staff — including angry outbursts and the use of slurs — drew criticism on Thursday from Republicans who suggested they showed her unfitness for the Senate seat she is seeking.

But it was not clear whether Alaskans, who for decades have elected abrasive, bellicose and occasionally violent individuals to represent them in Congress, would find it disqualifying.

Alaska’s representatives on Capitol Hill have long brought a special brand of coarseness to Washington, part of a frontier mentality and a rough-and-tumble political tradition that comes with a bare-knuckled approach to securing federal resources for their remote state. They often seem to operate with a chip on their shoulder, arguing that their state’s distance leads to its getting short shrift.

“In Alaska, abrasiveness can sometimes read as political charisma, or sometimes even as authenticity, given that Alaska has a political culture that rewards independence,” said Alexander Hirsch, a political science professor at the University of Alaska Fairbanks. “What sometimes reads like irreverence in Washington, D.C., can simultaneously signal to Alaskan voters something that’s really politically attractive.”

Here is a look at a few of the state’s more aggressive characters.

Serving in the Senate for 40 years, Senator Ted Stevens was known as a fierce and often hot-tempered advocate for Alaska. As a member and then chairman of the powerful Appropriations Committee, he funneled billions to his state, including to create the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, which made the state rich. Republicans made Mr. Stevens their second-highest ranking official in the Senate in 1977, a position he held for eight years.

An Army pilot during World War II, Mr. Stevens moved to Alaska in 1953 to practice law and soon afterward became the federal prosecutor there. He used to recount how he accompanied police on raids, gun strapped to his hip. In 1956, he went to Washington to work in the Interior Department on Alaska statehood, helping to bring Alaska into the union and then becoming a ferocious champion of it. He was named Alaskan of the Century in 2000 and a statue of him greets visitors at the Anchorage airport he showered with federal money and which is now named for him.

He was briefly convicted of concealing more than $250,000 in gifts by a federal jury in the District of Columbia in 2008, about a week before he lost a Senate re-election bid. About six months later, a judge threw out the conviction. He died in a plane crash in 2010, at 86, after surviving a serious crash in the 1970s.

When he faced a tough Senate debate, Mr. Stevens wore a tie featuring the image of the Incredible Hulk, the comic book superhero.

“I’m a mean, miserable S.O.B.,” he proclaimed in 1977 as he took over as chairman of the appropriations panel.

Decades later, Mr. Stevens once grabbed a reporter by the lapels in a Capitol hallway and urged him to help vanquish environmental activists who were thwarting his efforts to open a nature preserve to energy development. (The reporter did not.)

Angry that his daughters were not allowed to play Little League Baseball, Mr. Stevens became a fiery proponent of Title IX, guaranteeing gender equity in sports.

His temper was voted the “hottest” on Capitol Hill in a 2006 poll of congressional staff members by Washingtonian magazine.

Mr. Stevens did not argue with the characterization, instead boasting of how he used his hotheadedness to help his state.

“I didn’t lose my temper,” he once said. “I know right where it is.”

Gruff and irascible, Representative Don Young, who survived occasional allegations of shady ethics in his 49 years in the House, was a staunch opponent of environmental causes and a tough defender of Alaska’s oil, mineral and logging industries. He used his powerful leadership positions on two committees to fund highways, bridges, pipelines and many other projects. He passed away in 2022, at 88, while traveling home to Alaska.

Mr. Young moved to Alaska soon after it became a state and tried his hand at fishing, trapping and panning for gold. He was inspired, he said, by “The Call of the Wild,” the 1903 novel by Jack London about a sled dog in Alaska.

In Congress, he cultivated the image of a rugged frontiersman, and at times was crude in public. In a 1994 House debate on the right of Native Alaskans to sell sex organs of endangered animals as aphrodisiacs, he waved an 18-inch walrus penile bone at the face of the fish and wildlife commissioner.

In a radio interview in 2013, he referred to Latino migrant workers with an ethnic slur. In 2014, he forcefully grabbed a congressional staffer’s arm. In 2019, he shoved and cursed at a reporter. And in 2017, the former House speaker John Boehner of Ohio told Politico that Mr. Young had once pinned him against a wall in the Capitol and held a 10-inch knife to his throat, a story the Alaskan conceded at the time was “mostly true.”

His lapses rarely hurt him at the polls. He was elected to 25 consecutive terms, usually facing moderate to light opposition and winning more than 70 percent of the vote five times.

The former senator and governor was much less combative than the other two Alaskans and was overshadowed by Mr. Stevens in some ways. But he was known to be gruff and impatient in his pursuit of federal aid for the state. He left the Senate in 2002 when he was elected governor and he appointed his daughter, Lisa, a state lawmaker, to his seat in what many criticized as a blatant act of nepotism.

Ms. Murkowski went on to become a popular figure who used her positions on key committees to funnel federal money to Alaska and push for more oil drilling. She also had a thick skin, winning re-election in a write-in campaign in 2010 after losing the Republican primary to a Tea Party-affiliated candidate.

Ms. Murkowski, who remains in the Senate, is now known for cultivating an independent streak and breaking with her party on big issues, drawing the wrath of President Trump, whom she voted to convict at his 2021 impeachment trial.

In an Oval Office showdown in 2017, she told Mr. Trump her loyalty was to her state, not her political affiliation.

“With all due respect, Mr. President, I didn’t come here to represent the Republican Party,” she told him then, according to some of those present. “I am representing my constituents and the state of Alaska.”

item.title: Justice Jackson Calls Emergency Docket ‘Potentially Corrosive’
item.description:
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson on Thursday criticized the Supreme Court’s use of its emergency docket, saying that the court’s willingness to fast-track high-profile cases posed a threat to its standing among the American public.

The court, she said in a speech, “cannot expect the public to have faith in our judicial system if, without clear explanation, we are consistently greenlighting harmful acts” without a full hearing.

Justice Jackson told the audience that there was “a serious concern” that the Supreme Court’s handling of its emergency docket was “having an enormously disruptive and potentially corrosive effect” on the federal court system.

Her remarks came during an annual lecture hosted by the University of the District of Columbia’s law school aimed at honoring a commitment to civil rights and civil liberties. The crowd of several hundred people included students from the historically Black law school.

Her speech came about two hours after she had fielded the latest high-profile emergency application. That request came from the Trump administration, asking the Supreme Court to allow it to continue to rapidly deport immigrants to countries other than their own.

Justice Jackson did not speak directly about that case, but she pointed to other recent emergency rulings, saying that the court was now routinely using “truncated procedures” to weigh in on consequential cases.

Unlike the court’s routine so-called merits docket, where cases are considered by the justices over months and decided only after extensive written briefs and oral arguments, emergency docket cases are often decided quickly and without full briefing or argument.

The Trump administration has flooded the court with applications for emergency action — about 30 in President Trump’s first year in office alone. The court has granted many of those requests, allowing Mr. Trump to implement policies, technically on a temporary basis, while their legality is considered by lower courts.

All three of the court’s liberal justices have criticized the court’s handling of its emergency docket, which critics call “the shadow docket,” but Justice Jackson’s speech on Thursday, which focused entirely on the subject, was particularly pointed.

It came after Justice Elena Kagan, another liberal justice, said publicly this summer that she thought the court had improved how it handled emergency requests, noting that more of the court’s emergency decisions now included some reasoning.

Justice Jackson nodded to the court’s recent emergency rulings, saying that the court “began to explain more.” She noted that it was “still not the full kind of explanation” given on the court’s regular docket, but added that she thought it was “a good and positive development.”

Still, Justice Jackson urged the court to reimagine how to handle the emergency docket, including coming up with a better system to decide whether to take up emergency requests and when.

She criticized what she called the court’s willingness to jump into cases before lower courts had decided them. The court’s “new approach,” she said, “often lacks any acknowledgment of the harms that follow when the Supreme Court consistently and casually divests the lower courts” of their authority.

Appointed by President Joseph R. Biden Jr. in 2022, Justice Jackson is the court’s newest member but has emerged as perhaps the most vocal public critic of its practices — in speeches and also in her written opinions.

She noted on Thursday that the court received thousands of normal petitions for review each year. Typically, it agrees to hear only about 60 of those. She worried aloud that the court could be perceived as failing to deliver equal justice.

“If we’re not careful, the emergency docket can and will become an end run around the standard review process, a special avenue that certain privileged litigants can use selectively,” Justice Jackson said. “Why is it that one party should get a fast pass to the Supreme Court of the United States when so many other parties are queued up, waiting patiently for the court’s attention?”

She said that “while it will sometimes be hard,” the justices could “patiently wait our turn” to take up cases once they had made their way through the lower courts.

The justice’s words were greeted with cheers and an ovation.

Across town, three of her conservative colleagues — Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr., Justice Amy Coney Barrett and Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh — had been invited to dine on sea bass and ice cream at a White House state dinner for President Xi Jinping of China.

item.title: Trump and Xi Exchange Symbolic Gifts Ahead of State Dinner
item.description:
President Trump and President Xi Jinping of China exchanged both pleasantries and symbolic gifts during a summit in Washington this week.

In remarks ahead of a state dinner at the White House on Thursday, Mr. Trump introduced a gift for Mr. Xi: a statue of a bald eagle, perched on a branch atop a podium.

Mr. Trump said the statue was designed “in personal collaboration” between himself and the first lady, Melania Trump.

“The bald eagle is a national symbol of the United States and an embodiment of the free and soaring spirit of America,” Mr. Trump said. “We hope it’ll find a nice place, a wonderful place, in Beijing.”

Mr. Xi rose from his seat to applaud the gift after Mr. Trump gestured toward him.

The Chinese president did not offer a gift in return during his toast. But earlier in the day, Mr. Xi had announced that China would send two pandas to Zoo Atlanta as “envoys of friendship.”

Pandas have long been diplomats for China. It sent two pandas to the United States shortly after President Nixon’s landmark visit to Beijing in 1972, when the first lady, Pat Nixon, told China’s premier, Zhou Enlai, that she loved the bears. Zoos in San Diego and Memphis have also hosted pandas, who are often sent home to China after periods on loan.

Zoo Atlanta sent a family of pandas back to China in October 2024 and had since been in talks to acquire another pair. For the first time in decades, there were no pandas in the United States. But Mr. Xi’s gesture on Thursday makes it official: The Atlanta zoo will soon receive Ping Ping, a male panda, and Fu Shuang, a female panda. Both were born in China in 2020.

item.title: Justice Department Scraps Dozens of School Desegregation Cases
item.description:
The Justice Department said on Thursday it had ended its watchdog role in more than 50 cases enforcing racial desegregation in schools, mostly in the Deep South, a significant milestone in the Trump administration’s bid to overhaul civil rights enforcement in America.

Justice Department records showed that 57 desegregation orders have been dismissed since the start of President Trump’s second term, although it could not be verified late Thursday that a judge had ruled in each one. Nearly 80 percent of the cases were in five Southern states — Alabama with five, Georgia with 15, Louisiana with 11, Mississippi with 13 and South Carolina with one.

“This is just the beginning,” Steve Marshall, the attorney general of Alabama, said in a social media post thanking Harmeet K. Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for civil rights, for ending “outdated orders” in his state. “We will keep working until every school district in Alabama is free from unnecessary consent decrees.”

Five of the dismissals were in Florida, and there was one each in Arkansas, Arizona, Connecticut, Missouri, North Carolina, Tennessee and Texas, according to department records.

The federal government’s policy pivot has been deeply polarizing, particularly among civil rights advocates and legal scholars who have opposed the shift.

Groups including the N.A.A.C.P. have said that desegregation orders do more than change the racial makeup of classrooms by mandating equal funding, access to high-quality facilities and fair representation in advanced placement programs.

“Schools are just as segregated today as they were in the late 1960s,” Democrats on the House Education and Workforce Committee said Thursday in a social media post, adding that the Trump administration was “turning us back toward the Jim Crow era.”

Segregation in schools has been on the rise in recent years, partly stemming from a 1991 Supreme Court ruling that made it easier for school districts to be released from court-ordered desegregation, according to a 2024 study published by the American Journal of Epidemiology. The study found that school segregation significantly affects racial disparities in children’s health.

But the Justice Department suggested that the desegregation cases were relics of the nation’s past that continued to impose unnecessary financial burdens on local governments.

“In some cases, school districts have been under federal control for more than 60 years,” Ms. Dhillon said in a statement. “Now these local school districts can redirect taxpayer dollars back to benefiting students, instead of funding onerous and outdated consent decrees.”

As of last year, more than 130 school systems were under Justice Department desegregation orders, according to court records.

The Justice Department assigned a pair of lawyers to review the desegregation orders case by case to determine whether the data showed evidence of racial unity.

“In this administration,” Ms. Dhillon said, “we are ending prolonged federal oversight of these school districts because the effort does not reflect the reality of those classrooms today.”

The desegregation cases trace back to the racial disparities that defined the Jim Crow era in the United States, when local laws — particularly in the South — effectively ensured segregation in public spaces. The Supreme Court cemented those laws with an 1896 ruling, Plessy v. Ferguson, which held that “separate but equal” public facilities were legal.

Segregation remained in place for decades until another Supreme Court ruling, Brown v. Board of Education in 1954, which determined that racial separation was unconstitutional.

In the aftermath of the Brown ruling, the Justice Department regularly took school districts to court to enforce the decision. Many of those cases resulted in consent decrees that required ongoing reporting from local school districts and monitoring from the federal government.

The bid to eliminate those consent decrees is just one front in the Trump administration’s broader push to reorient enforcement of civil rights law.

Mr. Trump has signed a spate of executive orders aimed at purging consideration of diversity, equity and inclusion, or D.E.I., a catchall term increasingly used to describe policies that benefit those who are not white men.

Other orders have targeted historically marginalized groups, along with the laws and court rulings in place to protect them. The Trump administration has abandoned civil rights cases in education, employment, housing and trade issues, while filing lawsuits aimed at prohibiting transgender athletes from playing on girls’ and women's’ sports teams and suing states to turn over voter registration data.

item.title: Pandas and Eagles and A.I., Oh My! Trump Throws a State Dinner for Xi
item.description:
It was just a fun little dinner for the people deciding the future of humanity.

The amount of power concentrated at the head table alone was dizzying. The American president and the Chinese president, dining by candlelight with Elon Musk, Jensen Huang and Tim Cook, all of them sitting in the State Dining room of the White House at this moment that many in Silicon Valley warn could be the last before mankind stumbles into the A.I. apocalypse.

Standing before a room chockablock with A.I. moguls, billionaires and politicians, President Trump decided to depart from his prepared remarks. Now that he finally had these people together in one place, he could talk about his important plans. The ones he’s been working on nonstop ever since he returned to the White House.

“If I could go off-script, just for a second,” he said.

The sound of rich people clapping filled the room. Suspense!

“I just want to say …” the president continued.

“… I’d like to invite everyone in the room to visit through that beautiful curtain in the back — The door, it’s all lit up, and looks beautiful. It’s one year away from completion, the new ballroom that you’ve heard about.”

Oh. He was inviting them to take a walk through the construction site in back of the house.

“You’ll be the first people to step foot on that,” he told guests including Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg and Sam Altman, “and we’ll do that maybe after we’re finished with the entertainment tonight.”

There was not a single mention of A.I. in his speech. Mr. Trump doesn’t buy into the A.I. panic. He insists it’s mostly just a problem of branding. A.I. needs better P.R.

If any of the tech titans and members of Chinese Politburo who showed up to the White House used the state visit to get on the same page about the direction of this terrifying new technology, they haven’t shared their designs with the public. This was a roomful of people who have many disagreements about the way forward.

The American president, for his part, just seemed happy to be playing maître d’ to the mighty.

“You will see something that I think you will really love,” Mr. Trump told them about the ballroom site. “Tonight, if we had it, we would have had way more than a thousand people, with standing room only. And this room has about 145, that’s about it.”

“Anybody who wants to walk into a construction site that’s nice and clean and sparkling, it’s our honor to have you do so,” he said. “This is in honor of President Xi, Madam Peng.”

Mr. Trump never seems more pleased than when he is hosting wealthy and powerful people at his table. The aspects of the job that so clearly delight him concern pageantry and set design, and Mr. Xi’s visit provided opportunities for plenty of it.

Earlier in the day, Mr. Trump took Mr. Xi around the back to show off a new helipad and the slick new driveway. “He’s an expert on stone, aside from many others, and he loves good granite,” Mr. Trump told reporters as the pair walked back inside.

Mr. Xi announced a gift of two giant pandas, named Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, who will live at the Atlanta zoo. At the dinner, Mr. Trump unveiled a rather large statue of a bald eagle to give to the Chinese autocrat.

“We hope it’ll find a nice place, a wonderful place, in Beijing,” Mr. Trump said.

Sadly for Mr. Trump, almost none of this made it onto the television networks he watches so closely. The Chinese state visit has collided with the consequences of the decision he made in a fit of pique last Friday to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House campus. A judge ordered the Trump administration to let the banned reporters back Thursday, but the TV networks are still refusing to take Mr. Trump’s carnival live. Until his administration formally agrees to let CNN back into the White House TV pool rotation, he is not going to see those blinking red lights he loves so much.

Shortly before the dinner began, he posted one of his diatribes on his website.

CNN and MS NOW were “fake,” he wrote, because they wouldn’t cover “one of the Biggest and Most Beautiful Events to take place in many years, the arrival at the White House of the Highly Respected President of China, Xi Jinping, and his beautiful wife, Madam Peng."

The president continued: “The event was magnificent — Actually made for Television but, because they’re Fake News, and because they knew how good it would be, they didn’t want credit to be given to ‘TRUMP,’ they refused to be there. That’s why they have such poor Ratings.”

He concluded: “Tonight’s State Dinner at the White House, for President Xi, will be spectacular! The Media will be in attendance.”

Yes, the White House complex was crawling with journalists Thursday evening as Mr. Xi pulled up to the front door of the residence. But, in the spirit of solidarity with those targeted by Mr. Trump’s ban, some just ignored the spectacle.

item.title: A Quiet ICE Surge That Unfolded ‘Everywhere All at Once’ This Summer
item.description:
The most effective escalation of President Trump’s mass deportation campaign happened quietly.

Unlike earlier high-profile raids that drew thousands of protesters into the streets of Chicago, Los Angeles and Minneapolis, the surge in arrests in June, July and August was captured mostly by grainy security camera footage, through cracked blinds and from behind closed doors.

Arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement this summer soared to record highs since the start of this Trump administration — with 43,000 in June, more than 49,000 in July and nearly 51,000 in August — as officials cut or narrowed the pathways to legal residency in the United States and expanded the pool of people eligible for deportation.

Federal agents appeared in nearly every corner of daily life, carrying out operations at hospitals and airports, outside suburban schools and along rural construction sites and truck stops. They fanned out from coastal cities in Maine to desert towns in Arizona, across the open plains of Wyoming and down through the southern borderlands.

In Republican-led states like Texas and Florida, where the swell was strongest, they amplified their reach through partnerships with sheriffs and state highway patrol officers. In Democratic strongholds, they intensified their activities despite laws meant to restrict them.

David Bier, director of immigration studies at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank, said the local partnerships, an infusion of federal dollars and new technology had made the dragnet so decentralized that it had attracted less attention.

“This gradual rise everywhere all at once, through a lot of means, is enabling the operation to fly under the radar,” he said.

The spike in arrests, to little public backlash, reflects a turning point in the Trump administration’s efforts to carry out large-scale expulsions of noncitizens. Those arrested were accused of violating civil immigration laws, but most had not been charged with or convicted of a crime. In a statement, ICE defended the expansion of immigration enforcement.

“This is promises made and promises kept in action,” the statement read. “The results speak for themselves.”

To understand how the operations have unfolded around the country, The New York Times reviewed arrest videos, photographs and court records from more than 50 incidents. What follows is a sampling of those interactions.

Federal agents appeared as people carried out their everyday routines. People were detained en route to a soccer match. Leaving Sunday Mass. Having a drink at a nightclub. At national forests and outside polling locations.

Roger Hansen, 83, owner of the Little Big Load Laundromat in Madison, Wis., said federal immigration agents took five people from two of his locations in June. Statewide sweeps the same day resulted in the arrests of roughly 40 people, many of whom Department of Homeland Security officials said had criminal charges for sexual assault, driving while intoxicated and other crimes.

Security footage from one of Mr. Hansen’s laundromats shows two agents slamming a young customer to the ground near a soap dispenser. All the while, people continue to do laundry.

Outside, bystanders recorded the man being walked out in handcuffs and loaded into an S.U.V. with dark-tinted windows.

Mr. Hansen said he was disturbed by the violence. “They were having a heyday beating up on a kid,” he said, adding that business had dropped roughly 50 percent the next day and had not recovered. He said he believed many of his Latino and immigrant clientele may be too afraid to return.

In a statement, ICE said the arrests at the laundromat had been part of “targeted operations” in Wisconsin at the end of June. The five people from Nicaragua and Mexico were in the country illegally, ICE said. The agency did not respond to a question about their criminal records.

On July 7 in Salt Lake City, Elizabeth Garcia recorded three ICE agents forcing their way into her home without showing a warrant after following her father, Raul Moreno Meza, 52, from a gas station.

In the video, agents handcuff Mr. Moreno and his 15-year-old son, a U.S. citizen. Ms. Garcia howls and pleads as agents carry her father outside to their vehicles. Her 2-year-old can be heard crying in the background.

Before departing, an agent removed the shackles from Mr. Moreno’s son, who chased the S.U.V.s as they drove away. Mr. Moreno was later released on a bond, his daughter said, but her brother has become withdrawn and is attending therapy.

“He had lots of goals and intentions,” she said. “Now he is so negative.”

In a statement, ICE said officers arrested Mr. Moreno after he did not yield to officers at a traffic stop and then fled on foot. The agency alleged in the statement that “a juvenile occupant of Moreno’s vehicle” had assaulted an officer and was “detained in handcuffs for safety.”

Mr. Moreno, an undocumented Mexican man, crossed the border unlawfully about two decades ago, after his green card petition languished in delays and as his father, a naturalized U.S. citizen, fell ill, his family said. His father later died. Because Mr. Moreno’s green card petition was tied to his father’s citizenship, the application did not advance after the death, the family said.

Immigration arrests climbed to near record highs in almost every state. Some of the sharpest percentage increases in daily arrests occurred in Oregon, Montana, Hawaii, New Mexico, Vermont and New Jersey.

In June, the dragnet came to Harrison, N.J., where Asian and Hispanic residents account for about 65 percent of the population.

Tugrul Ozkarsli, 33, of Turkey, had just pulled up to his home with groceries when ICE agents in plain clothes boxed his vehicle in with their S.U.V.s, his wife, Kendra Ozkarsli, 46, said. He honked his horn and called her from his phone.

“All I hear is him screaming,” Ms. Ozkarsli recalled. She ran downstairs to find agents pulling him out of the vehicle.

“I’m married!” Mr. Ozkarsli yelled as agents handcuffed him.

“What are you doing? What are you doing?” Ms. Ozkarsli repeated, her hands shaking as she recorded with her phone. “This is my husband! Please stop!”

Mr. Ozkarsli had entered the United States legally on a business visa in December 2024. Before it expired, he applied for a student visa, which is still pending, Ms. Ozkarsli said. ICE said the pending application did not give him legal status.

The agency also said he had been arrested on burglary charges in New York last year. Ms. Ozkarsli said he was arrested after he entered the apartment of a woman he was dating at the time to retrieve his wallet and passport, prompting the woman to call the police. The charges were ultimately sealed and dismissed, she said.

Mr. Ozkarsli and Ms. Ozkarsli had married this summer, and he had been preparing to apply for a green card, she said.

Traffic stops were central to the summer surge. Some were deadly. In Houston and Biddeford, Maine, traffic stops ended in fatal shootings involving officers. An encounter between people in a vehicle and agents at a Florida gas station resulted in a fatal car crash.

In Milwaukee, Frankely Quezada, 34, and Estenderly Marte Polanco, 31, of the Dominican Republic, were running errands with their 7-year-old son on a Saturday morning in June. Near home, Mr. Quezada said, he noticed an unmarked S.U.V. trailing his van. He turned into an alley and accelerated.

The vehicle behind him flashed its lights, and as Mr. Quezada crossed the street, more S.U.V.s emerged to box him in. Federal agents jumped out, and one of them pointed a yellow stun gun at him and shattered his window, Mr. Quezada recalled. From a balcony, a neighbor filmed officers dragging Ms. Polanco out as her son cried.

Mr. Quezada, who was not arrested, said Ms. Polanco bit a federal agent as they drove her away after he shoved her face into her lap so forcefully she believed she would suffocate. Ms. Polanco, who overstayed a visa and has no other criminal record, remains held without bond in Kansas.

In response to questions about Ms. Polanco’s arrest, ICE said in a statement that both Mr. Quezada and Ms. Polanco had been combative and refused to obey commands and that Ms. Polanco would remain in custody as her case moves through immigration proceedings.

ICE also stepped up its arrests of foreign citizens at airports in July, in encounters that could be more surreptitious. Footage recorded by an airline manager on July 13 captured two ICE officers in plain clothes approaching a gate agent at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport before a flight to Portland, Ore. They identified themselves only as federal officers and instructed the employee to page a passenger.

Flanking the woman, the men discreetly took her into custody, according to the manager, who asked not to be identified, citing concerns for her job. The worker followed them, recording as they escorted the passenger through the concourse, one of them wheeling her luggage.

In the parking lot, the woman was handcuffed and put into an unmarked vehicle.

ICE agents told the manager that the woman was being detained because she had overstayed her visa. U.S. authorities did not share her name with The Times or provide information about her whereabouts.

During the summer surge, displays of force were routine inside some courthouses, and federal agents have increasingly been spotted at and near hospitals and schools.

ICE acknowledged operating in courthouses but said officers did not target schools.

“Nothing in the Constitution prohibits arresting a lawbreaker where you find them,” the agency said in a statement. “The ability of law enforcement to make arrests of criminal illegal aliens in courthouses is common sense. It conserves valuable law enforcement resources because they already know where a target will be.”

On the morning of Aug. 20, Grace Calero, 39, and her daughter, Giulianna Carriel, 19, were rushed to a hospital after a car crash south of Orlando, Fla. As medical staff treated them for injuries, a federal agent entered the emergency ward and began questioning Grace’s sister, Gia Calero, about the women’s immigration status, the sister said.

He remained in the room, joking with nurses.

It wasn’t until hours later, after Grace’s neck brace was removed, that the officer announced he was with ICE, Gia said. In the dramatic scene, captured by Gia on her cellphone, five deputies with the Polk County Sheriff’s Office arrived. They handcuffed Grace as Giulianna wailed on a bed, clinging to her mother and begging them not to take her.

“They didn’t even let them recover,” Gia Calero said.

In statements, ICE and Polk County sheriff’s officials said the women had overstayed their visas. Gia said her sister and niece had pending asylum claims, stemming from attempted kidnappings in Ecuador. The two have since been deported to their native country.

item.title: New Film Revisits One City’s Deadly Chapter of ‘To Catch a Predator’
item.description:
Chris Hansen spent years on TV confronting men about behavior they hoped would stay hidden. Now a new film is turning the camera back on one of the darkest episodes of “To Catch a Predator,” the NBC series he hosted from 2004 to 2007.

“Primetime,” an A24 film starring Robert Pattinson as Mr. Hansen, revisits a 2006 sting operation that “To Catch a Predator” carried out with the Murphy Police Department. The operation culminated in the death of Louis W. Conradt Jr., known as Bill, an assistant district attorney who killed himself after the police and camera crew arrived at his home in nearby Terrell, Texas.

“It’s tragic that somebody would take their own life,” Mr. Hansen told The Times about the incident.

For some of the people who lived through the episode and remain in Murphy, the renewed attention from the movie, which is being released on Friday, is unwanted.

“Oh my God, why don’t they let this thing die and go away?” said Sam Love, a former Murphy detective who was there during the filming of the 2006 episode. “It’s been 20 years almost and here we are, still trying to make money off this story."

The sting brought a flood of news coverage, a multimillion-dollar lawsuit against NBC, a documentary — and now, the feature film, which is already generating Oscar buzz for Mr. Pattinson.

In a statement, NBC said, “The movie is a fictionalized portrayal of events from nearly two decades ago that were extensively reported at the time. Over its nearly 35-year history, Dateline has significantly evolved along with the television landscape.”

Walter Weiss, who goes by the nickname Gator, was another former detective at the scene in 2006. He recalled the damage caused by the TV episode.

“It left a trail of destruction through many lives, through the city of Murphy, through the Bill Conradt family because of the reckless handling of this,” he said in an interview.

Mr. Weiss said his involvement in the sting still weighs heavily on him — “a stain on my soul.” He wrote the warrant for Mr. Conradt’s arrest and facilitated the police’s entry into his house.

“I signed a piece of paper and a man died,” Mr. Weiss said.

At the time, Mr. Love and Mr. Weiss both worked in Murphy’s criminal investigations unit. They recalled their boss, Chief Bill Myrick, calling a departmental meeting to announce that they would be participating in an episode of “To Catch a Predator.”

The show, a recurring “Dateline NBC” segment that was presented as investigative journalism but more closely resembled reality TV, first aired in 2004. Adult decoys posed as underage children to lure alleged sexual predators to a house where hidden cameras recorded Mr. Hansen confronting them. Police officers often waited nearby to arrest them.

The stings were conducted in partnership with Perverted Justice, a now-defunct internet watchdog group that was composed of private citizens who posed as minors online. Mr. Hansen and his crew traveled to communities across the country, and by 2007, the show said it had caught more than 200 people, according to The Columbia Journalism Review. “To Catch a Predator” became one of the “Dateline” program’s most popular segments.

In an interview, Mr. Myrick defended the city’s decision to allow the operation in Murphy, adding, “My job was to put bad people in jail, and that’s all I ever did.”

Mr. Love said he felt uneasy as soon as Mr. Myrick announced the plan.

He wasn’t the only one. In a letter to the police department ahead of the operation, District Attorney John Roach said his team would take no part in it because his office was “in the law enforcement business, not show business,” the letter read.

“To Catch a Predator” set up its undercover operation in the fall of 2006 at a vacant house in Murphy’s Rolling Ridge neighborhood, one of the town’s most affluent enclaves, just a few blocks from an elementary school. Two-story homes of brick and stone lined the street. One resident recalled the TV crew had put up Halloween decorations.

As the alleged child predators arrived at the house, Mr. Hansen would greet them with his familiar line: “Why don’t you have a seat?” Police officers waiting outside would arrest them as they left.

“They would literally tackle them on the front yard and arrest them with their guns drawn and all that,” Mr. Love said.

The sting caused an uproar in the tight-knit community, which had about 12,000 residents at the time. Bret Baldwin, a psychologist who was serving as mayor, was given no warning about the sting. Suddenly, he was fielding dozens of calls, both for and against the operation.

Over the course of four days in Murphy, the crew made more than 20 arrests at the house. None of the cases resulted in a conviction, Mr. Weiss said.

Now two decades later, Mr. Weiss said he wondered whether the operation in Murphy was meant to enforce the law or boost ratings for NBC.

“Primetime” explores that question through its portrayal of Mr. Hansen, who appears obsessed by a desire to catch men seeking to exploit children and by the success of the show.

Mr. Hansen rejected the suggestion that TV ratings drove his work.

“We earnestly tried to conduct an investigation, collaborating with the Murphy Police Department, to find men who were trying to exploit children,” said Mr. Hansen.

As of Thursday morning, he had not seen the film. “From the trailer, except for the fact that Robert Pattinson uses my name and a couple of phrases I have used over the years,” he said, “nothing in that trailer actually happened in real life.”

But the film’s final scene is based on real life. Mr. Conradt, a respected assistant district attorney at the time, had reportedly communicated with a Perverted Justice volunteer, believing him to be underage.

When the TV crew could not persuade Mr. Conradt to come to the house in Murphy, they visited him in Terrell, a 45-minute drive southeast.

Mr. Hansen maintains that he did not force anyone’s hand. “We weren’t telling them it had to be done, and we weren’t putting any pressure on them,” Mr. Hansen said Thursday. “That was the police department’s decision.”

In the film, Mr. Conradt resides in a mansion with a broad staircase leading up to the front door. His actual home was a modest midcentury ranch house that was passed down through his family. He grew up there, and in 2006, lived there alone with his dog.

James Flanagan, Mr. Conradt’s neighbor at the time, still lives in the brick house next door. Now 81, he reached into the pocket of his overalls for a pack of Pall Malls as he recalled what he saw from his front porch all those years ago.

“The cameras were set up before any law enforcement officers got here,” Mr. Flanagan said.

Police officers waited while Mr. Weiss prepared a search warrant. He’d been awake for more than 24 hours, he recalled, and felt deeply conflicted but boxed in by orders from above. He said he tried to push back, arguing that because Mr. Conradt was an officer of the court, the Texas Rangers should be involved.

Mr. Flanagan watched as officers surrounded the house and entered through the rear. Some time later, a gurney carrying Mr. Conradt was rolled out, Mr. Flanagan said.

Mr. Conradt, who never married and had no children, was survived by his sister, Patricia Conradt. In July 2007, she filed a $105 million lawsuit against NBC. The last episode of “To Catch a Predator” aired that December. The lawsuit was settled in June 2008 for an undisclosed amount.

Ms. Conradt sold the family house in 2008. When work brought her back to town, she would sometimes drive past the home and see a cat sitting in what was her bedroom window.

“I wish none of this had happened and he was still here,” Ms. Conradt told The Times. “You just have to put your head down and go on.”

Mr. Hansen said he wouldn’t have done anything differently in Murphy, and he objected to the film’s characterization of him.

“It’s fundamentally unfair to use somebody’s name, image and likeness in a story that is intentionally false and dark and overly dramatic and fictional,” he said.

He added, “You have to ask the question: Is that ethical?”

Susan Beachy contributed reporting.

item.title: The Viral In-N-Out Spatula Hero Is Exactly Who You Imagined He Was
item.description:
It was a little before 1 a.m. and Luca Opperman was in his car in the In-N-Out Burger drive-through with his girlfriend, Haley Williams.

This was in Lake Elsinore, a city outside Los Angeles that looks a lot like other parts of the Inland Empire, if maybe a little bleak. This was the In-N-Out near the Walmart, not the other one. Everything was normal. Until it wasn’t.

They were sitting in the car — a Toyota Avalon roughly as old as Luca, a million miles on it, paint peeling off the hood. But inside the restaurant, something weird was happening.

A woman was in there screaming and bashing the counter with a tree branch. Luca, 20, didn’t know what had set her off or whether she or the workers were OK, but they were running for cover in their little red and white outfits.

“Don’t do it,” Haley told Luca. She knew what he was thinking.

“Don’t!”

But then he was out of the car, and up through the sliver of a drive-through window.

“Whoa!” said Pamela Alvarado, the woman behind them in the drive-through. She couldn’t believe that someone could shoot through a window that fast. She immediately thought of a scene in the Jackie Chan movie “Rush Hour,” where Chan slides through the impossibly small slot that bank tellers use to hand their customers cash.

Haley and Pamela squinted to see what Luca had grabbed off the counter to confront the woman.

It was a spatula.

When she was pregnant with Luca two decades ago, Lize Willers sensed that this would be an unusually active child.

There were the kung fu moves that her son seemed to practice, in utero, against her belly.

“You see these feet come out. You see these little elbows.”

He started zooming around on scooters when he was 3. By the time he was 11, Luca had already picked up sponsorship for the scooter tricks he had mastered.

His parents let him run wild. Some mornings, when he was a boy, Luca would greet his mother in her second-floor bedroom by running past her bed and jumping off the balcony, into the void, then landing on the lawn one story below.

He managed to do these jumps without breaking bones. His friends called him marshmallow because he was so elastic. But also — OK, mostly — because he was pretty chubby.

Luca played rugby, trained in taekwondo, constantly climbed trees and excelled at parkour, the extreme sport that involves using perfectly ordinary urban fixtures like benches, staircase railings and rooftops and perilously launching your body across them instead of walking down the sidewalk in the normal way.

He deployed his skills at all hours and in unusual places.

“Did he tell you the story where he flipped over Hunter Biden?” his mother asked.

He had not, in fact, told me the story where he flipped over Hunter Biden.

The kitchen was completely empty except for Luca and the lady. They circled each other like wrestlers in a ring. Each time the woman smashed the countertops it sounded like cymbals smashing.

There are a lot of good weapons in a fast food kitchen. Chef’s knives, grill scrapers, fryer baskets.

The spatula has a limited history as a weapon. In the very first episode of “SpongeBob SquarePants,” the titular hero uses a “hydrodynamic spatula with port and starboard attachments and turbo drive” to fend off a swarm of anchovies. But it is not an obvious choice.

So why did Luca grab the spatula?

He wasn’t sure. It’s a slapstick weapon if ever there was one. Crap.

Too late. He was in too deep. An angry woman swinging a tree branch was headed right for him. So the spatula it was.

The In-N-Out cooking staff had bolted so fast that there were burgers still sizzling on the griddle.

To understand the moment better, it might be useful to point out that the Inland Empire is the cradle of American fast food. The original McDonald’s is only an hour’s drive away. And these sterile, neon-lit places are accustomed to a level of chaos.

In the 1993 movie “Falling Down,” the world bore down against the character played by Michael Douglas. His car’s air conditioning fails, there’s terrible traffic — and the fast-food restaurant where he wants to order breakfast has just switched to lunch. He rampages across Los Angeles.

So while there was no way of knowing in that moment what might have prompted the woman to begin smashing up an In-N-Out after midnight on a weekday … it happens.

When they had arrived at the drive-through, Luca had ordered two burgers with grilled onions, spread and pickles, and animal-style fries, no cheese.

Haley had ordered a cheeseburger with chopped chilies and a side of fries. They had also asked for a cup of pickles as a sort of appetizer.

The pickles were the only part of the order that had been delivered before the commotion. So while her boyfriend was bobbing and weaving and waving the spatula, Haley was watching from the car, eating pickles.

Along the sun-drenched coast between Los Angeles and San Diego, there’s a subset of kids like Luca. They meet at trampoline gyms and find cliffs and bridges to somersault from. They call themselves flippers.

One of Luca’s friends lives in a van with solar panels that keep the air conditioning going. Another ditched a plan to attend law school to compete in world championships of freestyle trampolining. They travel great distances to find the best cliffs. Ali-Sina Khashimi, who works for AAA doing roadside assistance, has been to the North Shore of Oahu a couple of times with Luca.

Ali, as his friends call him, was sitting at home one morning when he saw a video on his social media feed of someone in an In-N-Out holding a spatula and squaring off against a lady holding a stick. He called Luca.

“I was laughing my ass off,” Ali said. “First Hunter Biden and now this.”

OK, the Hunter Biden thing.

In April, Luca and his younger brother, Alec, went to a show in San Diego put on by the journalist and documentary filmmaker Andrew Callaghan.

Callaghan’s events typically feature screenings, talent shows and a special guest. Hunter Biden was the guest.

During the talent show portion, a woman got strong applause for tying her shoelaces really fast. Then Luca stepped up.

“What’s your talent today, man?” Callaghan asked.

“I do flips.”

Someone in the audience laughed mockingly. “He does flips.”

Luca did a first round of flips across the stage, and his phone popped out of his pocket midair and hit him in the head. Awkward.

The audience gave him lukewarm cheers and applause. When Callaghan asked him to do another round, Luca leaned into the microphone.

“Can I flip over Hunter Biden?”

The crowd went wild, standing up from their seats and egging on Biden to come center stage.

Luca took a running start and launched over the former president’s son, flipping sideways.

The hundreds of people in attendance descended into pandemonium. Hunter Biden lifted his arms in the air and high-fived Luca.

When the show was over, Luca typed out an Instagram post with a clip. “Literally just sideflipped Hunter Biden.”

“Exactly what I expected you to be doing,” a friend responded in the comments.

The lady was still swinging the stick. Luca didn’t know what had set her off. It also wasn’t clear where she got the branch — the trees outside the In-N-Out there are all palms.

Haley was getting worried that her boyfriend was going to get smacked. Also she was running out of pickles.

Luca was still wielding his spatula, grease glinting on the edges of his meat-flecked, makeshift broadsword.

Then the woman turned around and started yelling at a couple of customers watching the standoff. Luca saw that distraction as his opportunity to strike.

He took a tilted stance like a defensive end before the snap, and then bolted toward her.

Lowering his shoulder, he rammed into her midsection. She fell to the ground and dropped the branch.

A shoulder check, Luca called it. He said it was inspired by his days playing rugby.

Pamela, in the car behind them, was relieved to see that the woman was not hurt, just disarmed.

The spatula had been a decoy.

Not long after, deputies from the Riverside County Sheriff’s Office arrived.

They arrested the woman and cited her for felony vandalism and brandishing a weapon, booked her into the county jail and released her.

What was she so angry about? the deputies asked the In-N-Out staff.

Her burger was cold, Luca heard one employee answering.

They had called her order number repeatedly but she didn’t come to get it. She had asked them to make a new one, Luca heard the employee say, but they declined. Next thing you know, she was back with the branch.

Few details have emerged about the woman, who public records indicate was 53, and neighbors say is a mother — part of a friendly family. They did not return calls or answer my questions at their door.

To the public, she’s one-dimensional — the lady who lost it at the In-N-Out. But whatever led her to snap that night, whatever she was dealing with, it was surely deeper than a cold burger.

After the deputies left, the staff cooked up a fresh order of burgers and fries for Luca and Haley.

They got back in the beat-up Toyota, unaware that Pamela in the car behind them had filmed the confrontation and that the video would soon go viral.

The internet loved it. The grumpy voices that fill social media came together in praise.

“Young man — may your burger always be double double, may your animal style fries always have the right amount of spread to cheese to onion ratio,” wrote one commenter. And “may you never have to wait longer than 10-15 minutes in the drive through line.”

His friends, of course, would tease him mercilessly over the spatula thing. The flipper with a flipper. Marshmallow’s greatest trick.

I’ve spent my career writing earnestly about wildfires or insurrections in faraway countries. So when a zany viral moment came across social media a couple weeks ago, I was intrigued when the national editor, Nestor Ramos, texted me. He proposed that we try to capture a moment in American life, a fast-food standoff in the dead of night. The idea was to write about it in the same humorous way people all over were responding to it. There was something distinctly American — and funny — about a guy jumping through a drive-through window and arming himself with a spatula.

Kitty Bennett provided research.

item.title: This Island Loves Its Bears. If Only They’d Stop Eating Trash.
item.description:
Kodiak Island, Alaska, draws tourists from around the world hoping to glimpse one of the planet’s most impressive apex predators. But lately, the island’s namesake brown bears have been gathering at a decidedly less scenic destination: the dump.

The bears have repeatedly breached the Kodiak landfill despite increasingly expensive efforts to keep them out, prompting state environmental regulators to threaten hefty fines and state wildlife biologists to warn that ending the influx is going to be expensive and complicated: The omnivores, the biologists say, can’t simply be pointed toward the island’s healthier offerings — like salmon, berries or deer — or killed.

Beaufort Sea

250 miles

Nome

Canada

Alaska

Anchorage

Juneau

Bering

Sea

Kodiak Island

Gulf of Alaska

The New York Times

The bears? They just want to eat junk food.

“Would you rather have a Snickers bar or a piece of broccoli?” asked Larry Van Daele, a retired Alaska state wildlife biologist. “They’re not so different than people in that way.”

Coexistence between animals and humans is a hard-won fact of life on the Kodiak Archipelago, a mountainous, windswept chain of islands in the Gulf of Alaska that is home to as many as 3,500 Kodiak brown bears, a cousin to Russian Kamchatkas and North American grizzlies that can weigh up to 1,400 pounds.

Bears are considered part of daily life on the island. Residents are encouraged to secure garbage and schoolchildren learn how to avoid confrontations with animals that have adapted well to living alongside them.

Perhaps too well.

“People who have lived here their entire lives will tell you that they had never seen a bear in town until about 10 or 15 years ago; they didn’t need to come eat garbage,” said Jared Griffin, the borough’s mayor. “But something has changed, and they’ve become much more of a nuisance.”

Bears have wandered onto the landfill since it opened in the 1960s. Recently — perhaps because smaller salmon runs and berry harvests have nudged them toward the enticing smell of human garbage — they found holes in the two-mile fence around the dump and essentially became adorable squatters.

Whenever borough workers patched the fence, these smarter-than-the-average bears dug under, climbed over or barreled through. Mr. Griffin said landfill crews once saw a sow throw a cub into the fence to see if it was electrified.

“There is no animal on earth like a Kodiak bear,” he said.

Several young bears have spent their entire lives at the landfill.

It’s “all they’ve ever known,” said Nathan Svoboda, a state biologist in Kodiak.

Last summer, cruise ships sent passengers hoping to see bears to the dump. “Bear jams” formed on the road by the landfill at dusk, when the animals emerged from hiding to dine on the garbage.

“It’s embarrassing,” said Aimee Williams, the borough manager.

On a recent afternoon, she explained that bears sometimes played in a storm water retention pond as she drove along the landfill’s main road. She rounded a corner and, sure enough, two bears were bathing in the shallow brown pool. Ms. Williams couldn’t help but gush.

“They shouldn’t be here, but they’re also so cute,” she said. “Look at their little heads!”

Fifty yards away, a landfill employee had also paused to watch. He waited to resume working until the bears shook themselves off and wandered into the foliage. Ms. Williams approved.

“Never turn your back on a bear,” she advised.

The spectacle is dangerous, especially for the bears. Mr. Svoboda has found solid balls of garbage in bear stomachs during necropsies, the result of a high-calorie, low-nutrition dumpster diet.

“They can essentially starve to death,” he said.

Tranquilizing and moving the bears doesn’t work. Two years ago, wildlife biologists flew a mother bear and cubs that had been raiding Kodiak garbage cans 40 air miles from the landfill to another island. Twenty-eight days later, they were back.

“Not just back in Kodiak,” Mr. Svoboda said, “back to the same exact dumpster.”

Larger and stockier than grizzlies, Kodiak’s bears were isolated on the island at the end of the Ice Age. For much of the 20th century, ranchers considered them a danger to livestock, an attitude summed up by a blunt local maxim: “If it’s brown, it’s down.”

Attitudes evolved, and federal authorities eventually set aside nearly two-thirds of Kodiak Island as a national wildlife refuge. Today, Kodiak bear tourism draws thousands, particularly in late summer and early fall when salmon crowd creeks and rivers, their fins cutting through the shallow water as they return to spawn and die — in some cases, by bears fattening themselves up for winter.

The borough has erected mesh wind guards around the landfill’s open cell to dissuade people from stopping to watch. It plans to hire an overnight guard and has installed motion-sensitive noisemakers to haze the bears with earsplitting sounds. Borough leaders plan to move the electric fence, which dips deep into stands of spruce and alder, closer to the garbage, giving bears fewer places to hide and workers better sightlines.

The idea is to make it as hard as possible for the bears to reach the garbage without busting the borough’s already-strained budget or driving up already-steep landfill rates.

Wildlife biologists say they expect a few bears will refuse to move and need to be killed. That will be poignant in a place where bears have gone from being hunted as pests to symbols of the island itself.

“These bears are sacred. If you don’t see God in them, you’re not looking,” said Leya-Anne Johnson, a Kodiak resident.

Most evenings, Ms. Johnson parks her car on Monashka Bay Road outside the landfill and talks to the magpies and bald eagles chattering overhead.

“You know there’s a bear coming, don’t you?” she asked them one recent night. “You warning your friends?”

A moment later, a bear trudged out of the trees and crossed the road, stopping 15 feet or so in front of her car to sniff the ground. He was close enough to smell, like a wet dog rolled in garbage, and not in any hurry.

“They’ve come up to the car before,” Ms. Johnson said in a whisper. “They don’t care we’re here as long as we mind our own business.”

The bear glanced at the car, pawed the ground again, then headed toward the landfill for dinner.

item.title: A Republican Under Pressure Sticks by Trump: ‘I Am Still With That Guy’
item.description:
If any Republican Senate nominee is sticking to the tried-and-true strategy of elections past — winning by embracing President Trump — it is Michael Whatley of North Carolina.

He spoke at Mr. Trump’s midterm convention. He stood by the Iran war. He opposed blanket pauses on building new data centers.

Some of his counterparts in other battleground states have been doing the opposite, seeking distance from Mr. Trump as prices surge and the president’s popularity keeps slumping. Not so Mr. Whatley, who welcomed visits last week and this week from Mr. Trump and Vice President JD Vance, a distinction no other Republican Senate candidate can claim.

“I am still with that guy,” Mr. Whatley said, referring to Mr. Trump while onstage last Wednesday in Gastonia, N.C., near Charlotte.

With six weeks to go until the election, Mr. Whatley is running out of time to win his bet that lashing himself to a president, whose ratings are near historic lows, to draw out the MAGA base will help more than it hurts. Mr. Whatley lags behind his Democratic opponent in polls, is at risk of losing critical funding from outside groups and is running for a Senate seat now seen as the likeliest in the country to flip in November.

Mr. Whatley may have no other choice.

Mr. Trump handpicked him to chair the Republican National Committee in early 2024, a job he held until last fall. Having never run for office, he entered the Senate race as an unknown to many voters, relying on his Trump ties to try to hold a seat in a state that Mr. Trump has won three times. He is seeking to replace Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican who has repeatedly disagreed with the president and decided to retire after Mr. Trump threatened him with a primary challenger.

Mr. Whatley tends to hold round-table events and news conferences with law enforcement, sometimes clad in a suit and tie. He is fluent in traditional Republican talking points about low taxes and increased public safety; standing next to Mr. Trump, he emphasized having backed the president when he was still a longshot candidate in 2015.

The challenge of embracing Mr. Trump is evident in the topics Mr. Whatley brings up as well as the ones he doesn’t. He has focused his campaign on crime — and has consistently trailed former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee, who has focused on the cost of living. Republican strategists are privately discussing whether to redirect financial resources away from the race, The New York Times has reported.

The day after Mr. Trump’s rally last week, Mr. Whatley told reporters in Charlotte that the president’s campaign push, along with millions in ad spending from allied groups, was working.

“Numbers are moving in our direction,” he said after an event with builders and contractors. He added: “We feel very good about this.”

But on Monday, with the days ticking down for Mr. Whatley to show that he can narrow Mr. Cooper’s lead, a Republican-aligned super PAC, Old North Action, removed $6.5 million in television ad reservations.

Republicans have still outspent Democrats in spending and future ad reservations in the race, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact. Mr. Whatley still has the support of Mr. Trump’s powerful super PAC. And Mr. Cooper, who has never lost an election, has never had to deal with such a well-funded Republican effort against him. North Carolina has three large media markets, helping make the Senate race one of the most expensive in the country this year.

Mr. Whatley, a former chairman of the North Carolina Republican Party, and Mr. Cooper, who was first elected to office in 1986, agree on one thing: Statewide races in North Carolina tend to tighten in Republicans’ favor.

A plurality of North Carolina voters are unaffiliated with either party; Mr. Cooper has noted that undecided voters tend to make up their minds late and lean Republican.

Mr. Whatley needs that trend to hold to keep Republican funding. Mr. Cooper needs to remind Democrats of past losses so that donors and voters do not become complacent. Although Democrats have held the governor’s office for most of the last 34 years, they have not won a Senate seat in North Carolina in 18 years. Mr. Trump has urged Republicans to vote as if he were on the ballot, trying to draw voters to the polls who typically vote only in presidential elections.

Despite Mr. Cooper’s lead and Republicans’ worries, neither the former governor nor other North Carolina Democrats dare to predict a Senate victory.

“People see the polls, and it looks like a blowout is forming,” said State Representative Jordan Lopez of East Charlotte, who has been campaigning for Mr. Cooper and other Democrats down the ballot. “But North Carolina has been 50-50.”

Mr. Tillis, who has not endorsed in the race, has said that Mr. Whatley should find ways to separate himself from Mr. Trump. Mr. Whatley has tried a different tack: changing the subject from the cost of living, which polls show to be the voters’ top concern.

According to Mr. Whatley, the “No. 1 issue” is crime. That has been a tough case to make with gas prices averaging more than $4 a gallon, and polls showing that the public has lost trust in Mr. Trump’s handling of the economy. In contrast, Mr. Cooper has spent six months campaigning under the slogan “Make Stuff Cost Less.”

“Remember, the president promised that cost of living would be the Day 1 focus,” Mr. Cooper told a crowd gathered last Friday evening at a Charlotte brewery. “Now that that’s not happening, the things they’ve done have made it so much worse.”

As a first-time candidate, Mr. Whatley, 57, has had to introduce himself to voters while also going after Mr. Cooper. He had an awkward moment in the event with Mr. Vance where he briefly struggled to finish a thought after a teleprompter glitch.

In a barrage of television ads, Mr. Whatley and his allies have blamed Mr. Cooper for a court-mandated pandemic-era settlement that granted 3,500 inmates early release from prison. They have also blamed him for the fatal stabbing last year of a Ukrainian immigrant on a commuter train in Charlotte, though the man accused in the murder was not released because of the settlement.

Mr. Cooper has dismissed the attacks as “lies” and fired back by tying Mr. Whatley to a convicted sex offender who held roles with the state Republican Party. Mr. Whatley has said he did not hire the man, calling him a volunteer who opposed his party chairmanship.

Mr. Cooper has also criticized Mr. Whatley, a lawyer, for his time as a Washington lobbyist for oil and energy companies, as voters are paying more for gas and electricity. When Mr. Cooper and the voter who introduced him at the Charlotte event last week mentioned Duke Energy, one of the nation’s largest utilities — which is based in downtown Charlotte — people booed.

Republicans contend that Mr. Cooper’s record as governor remains insufficiently examined. Mr. Whatley, Mr. Trump and Mr. Vance have pegged him as a “radical,” and Mr. Whatley has tried to use Mr. Cooper’s slogan against him, criticizing him as a tax-and-spend Democrat who “made things cost more.”

But some Republicans concede that most voters have a positive opinion of Mr. Cooper, 69, who is almost universally known to North Carolinians as a roll-up-his-sleeves centrist. Often in a blazer and button-down but without a tie, he campaigns with the demeanor of a community bank executive, his eastern North Carolina accent reminding voters that he worked summers on his family’s tobacco farm before becoming a lawyer and politician.

On the stump, he says he would roll back Mr. Trump’s tariffs, push to end the Iran war and pass anti-corruption laws. He rarely names the president.

“I will work with him when I can,” Mr. Cooper told reporters after his Charlotte event, “and I will stand up to him when I need to.”

Mr. Whatley told the builders and contractors gathered in a Charlotte high-rise that continuing North Carolina’s economic growth would require backing the president’s deregulation and tax policies.

When an attendee lamented that towns have imposed building moratoriums on new data centers, Mr. Whatley echoed Mr. Trump’s position that “we need to win the A.I. race,” while adding that data centers should work with communities to get local buy-in.

But Mr. Whatley spent more time talking about Mr. Cooper than about Mr. Trump. He argued that Mr. Cooper had bungled the initial response to Hurricane Helene, which devastated parts of western North Carolina two years ago. Last year, Mr. Trump appointed Mr. Whatley to help lead recovery efforts.

At the rally in Gastonia, Mr. Trump said his administration “spent more than $2 billion” on hurricane relief, though he noted that the state was waiting for more money.

“I’m going to get that to you, Michael,” Mr. Trump told Mr. Whatley. Then, he continued: “Now, if Michael loses, I’m not sending it, OK? No, I’m only kidding. You’re getting it. You’re going to get it, Michael.”

item.title: Alaskans Dismayed, but Not Moved, by Peltola’s Treatment of Her Staff
item.description:
Many Alaskans on Thursday largely brushed off the news that Mary Peltola, the state’s former congresswoman, had mistreated staff and used offensive slurs.

Although some said they were disappointed by Ms. Peltola’s behavior, voters appeared to have for the most part retreated to their partisan corners in the closing stretch of a key Senate race between Ms. Peltola, a Democrat, and Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican.

Republicans said Ms. Peltola’s behavior, documented in a New York Times article on Wednesday, was abhorrent and revealed poor judgment. Democrats closed ranks around her, insisting that flipping the seat was more important than personal character. Some even suggested that the image of Ms. Peltola upbraiding staff in Washington with profane language could bolster her blue-collar image in a hard-knock, independent-minded state.

“It doesn’t move the needle one iota for me,” said Cameron Sanders, a small-business owner in Anchorage who said his vote for Ms. Peltola was based on anger over tariffs and rising health care costs as well as a deep desire to boot Mr. Sullivan from office.

Alfred Sturmann, a retiree who was at the Fairbanks airport on Thursday morning, said he was skeptical of the claims made by former staff members of Ms. Peltola in the article, but “if it really is so, I would be a little bit disappointed that she would act like this.” Still, Mr. Sturmann said, he would vote for Ms. Peltola no matter what.

Ms. Peltola, who won an upset victory in 2022 to flip the state’s sole House seat to Democrats, has long been regarded as a warm and friendly presence in Alaska politics, well liked even by Republicans. But nine of Ms. Peltola’s former aides, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told The Times that she had a history of angry and profane outbursts directed at staff members and others. Some aides recalled times when she used a homophobic slur, and she was accused of shoving a staff member in her congressional office.

In text messages viewed and published by The Times, Ms. Peltola also used the word retarded to describe people, disparaged Planned Parenthood in offensive terms, and said that she hoped one of its board members “dies of a botched abortion.”

Ms. Peltola’s campaign has said many of the accusations made by former aides — including using the homophobic slur and shoving someone — were false or exaggerated, though it said she regretted her use of the word retarded. It also noted that many of the incidents described in the article occurred not long after the deaths of her mother and her husband in rapid succession in 2023. Her husband, Eugene, who was known as Buzzy, died in a plane crash.

“Like any person who has gone through multiple personal tragedies in the span of a few months, Mary sometimes struggled to deal with her grief,” Harry Child, a spokesman for Ms. Peltola’s campaign, said in a statement on Wednesday. “Exaggerating and outright lying about moments from the hardest period of her life, and falsely presenting them as a pattern of behavior, is wrong.”

Republicans seized on the news. Alex Latcham, the executive director of the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC that works to elect Republicans, said in a statement that the accusations against Ms. Peltola made her “entirely unfit for the U.S. Senate.”

And Mr. Sullivan, in an interview on Thursday, said he was saddened for the Alaskan staff members “who had to live with these experiences.”

“I think character matters in every race,” he said. “I think Alaskans expect their senator’s actions behind closed doors to be the same when they’re outside of closed doors.”

On Thursday, state Democrats sought to turn the page on the accusations made against Ms. Peltola, in part by making light of one staff complaint — that she had required them to feed live crickets to her family’s pet chameleon, Meatball.

“Alaskans everywhere wish Meatball well, and hope our state gets more coverage on things that actually matter,” the Alaska Democratic Party said in a statement.

Scott Kendall, an independent Anchorage attorney who once worked for Republicans but left the party in 2020, said he doubted the accusations against Ms. Peltola would reshape the contours of a race that hinged on economic conditions and the high cost of living in Alaska.

“The inherent irony here is you have a lot of progressives rushing to defend really, really unfortunate language that they would disavow in anyone else,” Mr. Kendall said. “And you have a lot of conservatives rushing to condemn language where if it came out of the president’s mouth or someone else’s mouth, they would say, ‘Don’t be so fragile.’”

On the left, some said they doubted the accusations. Others — especially online — embraced them, suggesting they portrayed Ms. Peltola as a tough operator and that it did not matter what she did as long as she helped usher in a Democratic majority.

“You can call me the f word as long as you win that seat we know you support us!!!!” one user replied to her on X.

Ashley Hensel, a health care worker in Anchorage, felt differently.

“One of the reasons that I vote Democrat, or I lean that way, is because I really feel strongly that we should create psychologically safe environments for people,” Ms. Hensel said. The words Ms. Peltola was accused of using, she said, “make other people feel small and less than, and I am not in favor of that.”

“It changes how I view her,” Ms. Hensel said. “It likely won’t change how I vote.”

item.title: Trump to Appear at Events in Oklahoma and Alabama
item.description:
President Trump is planning to rally in heavily Republican states over the next week as his party works to compete in battleground states to preserve its control of Congress.

Republicans said he would appear in Durant, Okla., on Thursday and in Mobile, Ala., next Friday. The Trump 47 Committee, his joint fund-raising vehicle with the Republican National Committee, will host both events.

Mr. Trump is also scheduled to watch the University of Texas play the University of Tennessee in Knoxville, Tenn., on Saturday afternoon, in the premier college football matchup of the weekend.

The president’s itinerary, about five weeks before the midterm elections, focuses on solidly Republican states and congressional districts. In 2024, for example, Mr. Trump carried 77 percent of the vote in Oklahoma’s Second Congressional District, which includes Durant. Meanwhile, nominees in battleground areas have poured tens of millions of dollars into tight races.

In those competitive areas, a growing number of Republicans are openly distancing themselves from Mr. Trump as they struggle with the declining appeal of the president and his signature policies.

Representative Ashley Hinson of Iowa, a Republican running for the open Senate seat in her state, skipped an appearance onstage at Mr. Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas and chose not to attend a rally last week headlined by Vice President JD Vance. Other candidates have chosen not to appear with Mr. Trump or have omitted his endorsements from their campaign ads.

This week, Republicans in tight Senate and governor races demanded an end to the war in Iran to try to undo the rise in prices of consumer goods and energy. Three other Republican senators called for an ethics inquiry into the president’s son Donald Trump Jr. over his lavish wedding after party, paid for by a Russian businessman with Kremlin ties.
