item.title: A Small Hawaiian Island Rode Out a Storm With Faith and Little Help
item.description:
It has been two weeks since Hurricane Lowell brought destructive winds and rain to the Hawaiian island of Kauai, but little is known about how it affected Niihau — a privately owned island to the west that was closer to the eye of the storm.

Niihau, about 70 square miles, is believed to be home to fewer than 100 Hawaiians. According to the 2020 census, the population was 84.

Officials with the state and Kauai County, which includes Niihau, have said they were in regular contact with the Robinson family, the island’s owners, as Lowell turned westward toward the main Hawaiian islands this month.

Niihau has maintained an unusual level of isolation since Elizabeth Sinclair of New Zealand bought the island from the Hawaiian king Kamehameha V in 1864 for $10,000 in gold. Two brothers, Bruce and Keith Robinson, who are her descendants and the island’s current owners, haven’t said anything publicly about storm damage.

No one is allowed to visit the island without the Robinsons’ permission.

“The damage assessment will take a little longer because we were very mindful about getting permission to go over to Niihau,” Gov. Josh Green of Hawaii said Wednesday during a news conference. “We humbly only go over when asked.”

Niihau has a subsistence-based, traditional culture that relies on rain catchment systems, solar energy, fishing and hunting. County officials said the island has sturdy structures, well-stocked supplies and a helicopter.

“They actually had a worse forecast than us,” Elton Ushio, administrator for the Kauai Emergency Management Agency, said in an interview.

The agency sounded an outdoor warning siren on Niihau on the evening of Sept. 7 as hurricane-force winds moved toward the island. The siren warned residents to stay indoors ahead of the imminent arrival of sustained winds of 74 miles an hour or greater.

Lowell knocked out power to most of Kauai and battered its north and south shores with flooding and storm surge. The Kauai police said there were two deaths during the storm. Eighteen homes were destroyed and 67 suffered major damage.

But there were no injuries on Niihau and everyone was accounted for, Mr. Ushio said.

“They told us about 30 were there for the storm,” he said.

No other details have been available.

“We, as well as the Robinsons, have been getting so much media questions,” Mr. Ushio said. “And they really try to be protective of their community.”

Members of the Robinson family didn’t return calls seeking comment.

Mr. Ushio said he had built a relationship with the Robinsons over his 33 years of working for the county. He has been to Niihau twice. In the 1980s, his father, a state Education Department employee, would jump on a barge taking supplies to Niihau every so often to check on the island’s school.

“They operate on a lot of old-school trust,” Mr. Ushio said. “In Hawaii, a lot of things is by trust.”

Whenever a storm threatens the county, the Robinsons, who also have significant land holdings on Kauai, participate in daily coordination calls, which include National Weather Service officials, utility leaders and the Federal Emergency Management Agency, Mr. Ushio said.

The Robinsons and the other residents of Niihau “are the toughest, most extraordinary people you’re ever going to meet,” Governor Green said. “They felt that they probably didn’t need any federal assistance because they are so resilient. They are used to living for generations independently.”

The Robinson brothers, who are in their 80s, are not Hawaiian but grew up fluent in the Niihau dialect of Hawaiian that is spoken on the island.

“The Robinsons are not considered outsiders,” said Hinaleimoana Wong, a Hawaiian cultural practitioner who lives in Honolulu. She is fluent in Niihau Hawaiian because she was taken in as a youth by a Niihau family, she said.

“They are not looked at by the Niihauans as the marauders, the plunderers, the raiders or the oppressive ones,” she said.

Niihau is an island of deep faith, she said. Missionaries introduced the Protestant branch of Christianity to Hawaii in the 19th century. On Niihau, they follow “kalawina,” or Calvinist theology, Ms. Wong said.

“When they received word that the storm is going to hit, they’re praying, they’re in church,” she said. “You have a Pacific island whose faith is greater than any storm.”

There are strict rules against tobacco and alcohol on Niihau, she said.

Hawaiian culture has remained far more intact on the island than in other parts of Hawaii that were transformed by U.S. colonization and the 1893 overthrow of the Hawaiian kingdom by a group of American businessmen.

“The Native Hawaiian community is always protesting, rallying, marching,” Ms. Wong said. “We got lots to grumble about because we suffered great degradation and loss of language, culture and history. But they didn’t.”

This week, the Kauai Island Utility Cooperative reported that service had been restored to 98 percent of customers who lost power during the storm.

Officials across the state were monitoring Hurricane Nolo, which was expected to bring heavy rain to the southern end of the Big Island that is still recovering from Hurricane Lala last month.

As of Thursday, the biggest rainfall threats from Nolo were to Maui and the Big Island, said Laura Farris, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Honolulu. Niihau was forecast to get 2 to 4 inches of rain, she said, and large waves could lash the island’s shores as Nolo moves west through Sunday.

Hawaii’s hurricane season generally goes through Nov. 30.

“Niihau will always survive,” Governor Green said, “but it was in the thick of the hurricane-force winds.”

Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: Polls Show Advantage for Incumbent Parties in 4 Governor’s Races
item.description:
Voters in four key battleground states largely prefer the incumbent party in their races for governor, according to New York Times/Siena polls in Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania.

The polls of likely voters found Gov. Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire, a Republican, and Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, a Democrat, each ahead by wide margins in their bids for re-election. Hannah Pingree, the Democratic nominee in Maine, also enjoyed a sizable lead in her bid to replace her fellow Democrat, Gov. Janet Mills, who is term-limited.

The New York Times/Siena poll

Sept. 15-22

Among likely voters. Shaded areas represent margins of error.

Based on New York Times/Siena polls of 605 voters in Michigan and 613 voters in New Hampshire, and on a New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll of 619 voters in Maine and a New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena poll of 615 voters in Pennsylvania.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

In Michigan, Jocelyn Benson, a Democrat, led by a more modest margin over her Republican challenger, Representative John James, in their race to fill the seat currently occupied by Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat who is term-limited.

Ms. Benson, Michigan’s secretary of state, leads Mr. James by five percentage points. That was around the same margin as the one held by Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in the state’s Senate race, though the poll found some meaningful differences in their support: Ms. Benson fares better with voters unaffiliated with a party, and, unlike Dr. El-Sayed, is winning voters over the age of 65.

Both candidates are underperforming relative to the state’s generic congressional ballot, in which voters are asked which party’s candidate they plan to vote for in their House district. On that question Michigan voters preferred Democrats by 10 percentage points — a significant shift in a state President Trump narrowly won in 2024.

Ms. Ayotte, a former Senator, is faring far better than other Republicans in New Hampshire, which leans Democratic in federal races but frequently elects Republicans to statewide office. She leads Cinde Warmington, a former executive councilor, by 11 percentage points thanks in part to bipartisan support she built in her first term as governor, which led to her winning 14 percent of registered Democrats and 18 percent of voters who say they plan to vote for a Democrat for Congress.

In Maine, Ms. Pingree leads by 13 percentage points over Bobby Charles, an attorney and lobbyist, with Rick Bennett, an independent state senator, polling at slightly under 10 percent. The result is virtually identical to Ms. Pingree’s margin in a June New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll — a remarkably stable result even as Senator Susan Collins, a moderate Republican, has taken a narrow lead in her bid for re-election.

Around 15 percent of Ms. Collins’s supporters also back Ms. Pingree for governor, slightly larger than the 11 percent who did so in the June poll when Graham Platner was still the Democratic nominee for Senate.

Finally, in Pennsylvania, the poll found Mr. Shapiro winning 58 percent of the vote against Stacy Garrity, the state treasurer, a broadly similar result to last month’s New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena poll of the race. Mr. Shapiro won nearly one in four registered Republicans, and is viewed favorably by more than 60 percent of voters.

item.title: Supreme Court Allows Federal Voter Identification Tool Ahead of Midterms
item.description:
The Supreme Court ruled on Friday that the Trump administration can deploy an expansive online system that combines citizenship information, Social Security numbers and other sensitive data about millions of Americans, including to allow states to use it to hunt for ineligible voters.

Critics fear that using the system could result in the purging of large numbers of valid voters from state rolls.

The majority concluded that a lower-court ruling that had blocked the Trump administration from rolling out the system was improper because it inhibited “the federal government’s efforts to assist state and local agencies in the proper administration of the midterm elections.”

The emergency ruling was unsigned and gave no vote count, but the court’s three liberal justices joined in dissent. The ruling was a victory for the Trump administration as it tries to marshal the resources of the federal government to shape who can vote, and how. The effort has prompted legal challenges ahead of November’s midterm elections.

In a 12-page dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson emphasized that the majority’s decision created the conditions for some states to cancel the voter registrations of at least some recently naturalized citizens or to force them to provide proof of citizenship before voting.

“The harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take,” she wrote, joined by Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan.

The decision came after the justices had dealt the administration a major setback this month, when the court’s majority blocked the government’s plan to require the Postal Service to screen mail-in ballots.

That loss frustrated President Trump, who assailed the court in a social media post, accusing it of “shockingly bad rulings that are of such magnitude that it won’t be easily possible for our Country to recover or heal.”

In March 2025, Mr. Trump signed an executive order directing several federal agencies, including the Department of Homeland Security and the Social Security Administration, to pool their records into an online tool that state and local officials could use to verify the citizenship and immigration status of registered voters.

It is illegal for noncitizens to vote in federal elections. Mr. Trump has long claimed, without evidence, that large numbers of noncitizens have managed to register and then illegally vote.

Mr. Trump’s directive prompted the Department of Homeland Security to overhaul the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements system, which had long been used by local, state and tribal agencies to check the citizenship and immigration status of people seeking some types of benefits and licenses. The expanded system pulled in Social Security data and other records.

Several legal challenges followed, including a lawsuit by voting rights groups.

In June, a federal judge in Washington blocked the Trump administration from allowing states to use the online system to screen their voter rolls.

Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan, who was appointed by President Joseph R. Biden Jr., found that in “scrambling to comply with an executive order aimed at reshaping federal elections,” federal agencies “haphazardly combined and repurposed the private information of millions of Americans, including citizenship data that they knew to be unreliable.”

Nicholas Nehamas and Ann E. Marimow contributed reporting.

item.title: Bracing for Midterm Losses, Republicans in Congress Try a Pre-election Pivot
item.description:
With less than 40 days until the midterm elections, Republicans in Congress are distancing themselves from President Trump and scrambling to show they are working to address the high cost of living, concerned that their failure to do either so far may cost them their majorities in November.

Mr. Trump’s approval ratings are sagging as Americans face higher energy costs and general economic uncertainty because of the war in Iran, giving Democrats a clear advantage in national polls. But the Senate has spent some of its final days in session ahead of the election defeating a bid to halt the war and working on a sweeping new regulatory framework for collegiate sports.

Even its proponents said it was an ineffective closing message at a time when voters are panicked about the skyrocketing price of gas, diesel and groceries — all factors that Mr. Trump has dismissed — and are opposed to the war with Iran that Republicans, with few exceptions, have allowed the president to conduct without their authorization.

“We’ve been spending all week on trying to make the football coaches happy,” Senator John Kennedy, Republican of Louisiana, vented to reporters on Thursday. “I can assure you that moms and dads out there across America, when they lie down to sleep at night, they’re not worried about the football coaches.”

Mr. Kennedy had been clamoring for months for the Senate “to do more on cost of living,” he added, “because we haven’t done a damn thing — and it’s biting us in the ass right now.”

That assessment, shared by many of his colleagues, has sent Republicans into a low-grade panic as they cast about for legislation they can quickly take up and pass in the coming days that could redeem them in the eyes of voters. The sense of desperation was driven home during a private luncheon this week at their political headquarters on Capitol Hill, in which G.O.P. senators were shown a grim assessment of their standing with voters that has placed them at risk of losing control of both chambers of Congress.

Under pressure to salvage his party’s chances, Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the majority leader, said on Thursday that he would keep the Senate in session for an extra week to bring up a House-passed bill aimed at addressing widespread voter anxiety about artificial intelligence. The legislation places no limits on the industry but would encourage states to consider requiring data centers to pay their own electricity bills rather than pass those costs on to consumers.

Mr. Thune may also seek to move on other measures intended to appeal to voters’ distrust of and disgust at Washington. One option would be to consider legislation that would limit the ability of members of Congress to trade stock. Punchbowl News reported earlier that it was under consideration. But that bill, which passed the House earlier this year, has been panned by Democrats. They said it had loopholes so big as to render it virtually meaningless, and in effect only blunted momentum for a more stringent measure that has bipartisan support.

It is all part of a rapid pre-election pivot Republicans are laboring to make, after more than a year of staying in lock step with Mr. Trump and his agenda, to protect themselves from a public backlash against the impact of his policies.

Many frustrated Republican lawmakers struggled this week to point to any recent accomplishments, reaching all the way back to the summer of 2025 and invoking the passage of the president’s “big, beautiful bill” as their singular achievement. But even that measure, which included tax cuts they love to talk about, contained drastic cuts to Medicaid and food assistance that have been politically problematic and deeply unpopular.

Mr. Thune flashed his frustration with the situation in a speech on the Senate floor on Thursday in which he blamed Democratic obstruction for his party’s inability to advance major legislation.

He noted that Senate Republicans and the Trump administration had given considerable ground on a major proposal to ease government permitting rules on energy projects, which he said would lower energy bills, but that Democrats still would not sign off on the deal despite months of bipartisan talks.

“What they really care about is denying Republicans another legislative win,” he said. “Hard-working Americans take a distant back seat to Democrats’ political priorities.”

He accused them of “throwing up every roadblock they can” for 21 months to block Republican legislative wins.

Lawmakers like Senator John Cornyn, Republican of Texas, said the passage of the data center legislation would count as action on cost-of-living issues that G.O.P. candidates could promote with voters. But many Senate Democrats planned to oppose the bill, calling it toothless because it lacked an enforcement mechanism. The bill is sponsored by Senator Jon Husted, Republican of Ohio, who is facing a tough re-election race and has struggled to address the data center issue.

“It’s not good enough to have something that is voluntary but not mandatory,” Senator Andy Kim, Democrat of New Jersey, said in an interview. “It doesn’t meet the moment for the American people, but maybe they think it meets the moment for what Senator Husted needs.”

He said Republicans were foolish to think they could persuade voters that they had done anything to address their main concerns.

“Everything is baked in already,” Mr. Kim said. “There’s no new message that will be able to penetrate through so much noise right now.”

Even some Republicans conceded that the electricity rate measure would do little to change the dynamics of the midterm elections.

“If people are doing it under the assumption that it creates a sea change, I just don’t buy it,” said Senator Thom Tillis, Republican of North Carolina, who is not seeking re-election.

For Republicans, the problem is not just failing to deliver any meaty agenda to lower costs. It is that they had actively cheered for things that most voters are furious about. Over and over and again on Thursday, they have voted against halting Mr. Trump’s unpopular war in Iran, which has led to higher gas prices and grocery costs.

“They have a record,” Mr. Kim said. “It’s just a record the American people are disgusted by.”

In the House, Democrats noted derisively that Republican leaders had sent their members home from Washington early rather than stay in session and be forced to take a politically tricky vote on whether to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

“Another decision made by House Republican leaders to get out of town before sundown as opposed to solving problems of importance to the American people,” said Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, who said Republicans were “running scared.”

Mr. Cornyn, who lost his primary this year to a Trump-backed challenger, said he believed his party had some accomplishments to be proud of, but conceded they were “not as much as I wish we could have.”

When asked to detail what Senate Republicans had to show for themselves after almost two years in power, Senator Kevin Cramer, Republican of North Dakota, named the tax cuts and efforts to curb undocumented immigration.

But then he found himself at a loss, noting that the major accomplishment of the past few months has been a stopgap spending measure to prevent the government from shutting down until after the November elections.

“We’ve had a lot of hearings,” he said. “Going home with a continuing resolution to get us through the election is a pretty strong demonstration that we’re not very functional.”

Still, he landed on the point that many Republicans are resorting to as they make the case for remaining in power: Democrats would be worse.

“The other thing we get to talk about is that at least we’re not socialists,” he said.
